t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we consider the ethical problems connected with the genome, gene therapy, stem cells and cloning, as well as questions of biosafety. The aim is to learn to analyse in depth, from the ethical standpoint, both the benefit and the risk of the achievements of genetics. The plan: genetic prognosis, gene therapy, the Declaration on the Human Genome, and questions of stem cells and cloning. Outcome: the student can explain the need to analyse the consequences of new technologies in advance.

t: Study of the genome and genetic prognosis
n: After the genome was studied in depth, the possibilities for diagnosing and treating hereditary diseases expanded. The chain is as follows: the human genome is studied, genetic diagnostics expands, genetic prognosis appears, and it becomes possible to know a risk in advance. Genetic prognosis makes it possible to determine a risk before any sign of disease appears, even before the child is born. Attention: a prognosis shows a future risk; it is not yet a diagnosis of a disease that has begun.

t: The twofold danger of a great discovery
n: A great discovery carries a twofold danger. In the first half of the twentieth century discoveries in nuclear physics brought great benefit but also gave rise to serious danger. The negative consequences became known after the atomic and hydrogen bombs were used in war, that is, at Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and after the Chernobyl disaster. In the view of the Nobel laureate Jean Dausset, applying the discoveries of genetics without deep theoretical analysis may lead to catastrophe. Therefore modern biogenetic research must be analysed deeply from the ethical standpoint.

t: Biotechnology's possibilities for health
n: Biotechnology opens bright prospects for preserving human health and treating disease in conditions of ecological crisis. It is possible to obtain the proteins needed for drugs such as insulin, somatotropin, interferon, vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. New methods are being developed that direct drugs only to the affected area. Gene technology makes it possible to map the genome and, with gene probes, to detect more than ten serious diseases in the embryo. The trends: drug production, targeted delivery, hereditary diseases, and also ecology and food.

t: Dausset's warning: biological restriction
n: Jean Dausset, a Nobel laureate, warns: a technology whose consequences have not been analysed may be tragic for humankind. Follow the chain: a new genetic discovery leads to genetic prediction, prediction becomes a means of controlling life, and this leads to biological restriction and the danger of loss of freedom. That is, genetic prediction may become a medical and biological means of controlling a person's life and biologically restrict his freedom. Attention: genetic prognosis is not the same as disease. It shows a future risk, and clinical signs may be absent as yet.

t: Case analysis: genetic prognosis and freedom
n: Case analysis. A genetic examination before the birth of a child showed which diseases threaten him in the future. The benefit is that the possibilities for diagnosing and treating hereditary diseases have expanded and it has become possible to know the risk in advance. The danger is that the prediction may become a means of controlling a person's life and biologically restrict his freedom. Question for discussion: is this prediction help for the child or a restriction? Justify your answer with arguments from the source.

t: Gene therapy: two methods
n: Gene therapy is carried out by two methods: through somatic cells and through germ cells. In somatic therapy a mutant gene is replaced with a healthy one. The change concerns only this person and is not passed on to offspring, and therefore is ethically harmless to the person. In germ-cell therapy the hereditary material of the germ cells is changed, and this is passed from generation to generation. Attention: a change in germ cells is passed to offspring, which is why UNESCO prohibited it for the time being in 1994.

t: Somatic therapy and fetal therapy
n: The first method of gene therapy is somatic cell therapy. In it a mutant gene is replaced with a healthy gene, and some successful results have been achieved. If heredity is changed in a somatic cell, the result concerns only that person and does not affect offspring. Therefore the somatic method is regarded as ethically harmless to the person. In fetal therapy, by contrast, the cells of the foetus are used. Not a few interpret this as a violation of traditional rules of morality and ethics.

t: Germ-cell therapy and the UNESCO ban
n: In the second method the hereditary material of the germ cells is altered. The chain is as follows: the germ cell is altered, the change is passed to the next generation, and affects the fate of offspring. For this reason UNESCO, that is, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, categorically prohibited it for the time being in 1994. The main idea here is that such changes are passed from generation to generation and affect the fate of future generations.

t: Attention: somatic therapy ≠ germ-cell therapy
n: Attention: somatic therapy is not the same as germ-cell therapy. The risk of error: assessing both methods in the same way. The main difference is whether the change is passed to offspring. The somatic method concerns only one patient, whereas the germ-cell method also concerns future generations. The consequence for offspring: with the somatic method it is not passed on, with the germ-cell method it is passed on to generations. Ethical assessment: the somatic method is harmless to the person, the germ-cell method requires deep ethical analysis. Reproductive intervention depends on the fate of generations. Status of the ban: in 1994 UNESCO prohibited the germ-cell method for the time being.

t: Quick question: gene therapy
n: Quick questions. Which method is passed on to offspring? The method in which the hereditary material of the germ cells is altered. These changes are passed from generation to generation. Why is it prohibited? It affects the fate of future generations, and in 1994 UNESCO categorically prohibited it for the time being. And somatic cell therapy? The result concerns only this person and does not affect offspring, so it is ethically harmless. Attention, there is a risk of error: somatic cell therapy is not the same as germ-cell therapy. The first is not passed on to offspring, the second is.

t: Case analysis: choosing gene therapy
n: Case analysis. A hereditary disease has been identified in a family. The physician is considering the method of replacing the mutant gene with a healthy gene. In somatic cells the change concerns only that person and does not affect offspring, so the method is ethically harmless. A change in germ cells is passed to generations and is prohibited by UNESCO. Some regard the use of foetal cells as a violation of morality. Question: which type of cell is ethically acceptable for this family, and why? What consequences would choosing the germ-cell method lead to?

t: The UNESCO Declaration: chronology of adoption
n: Chronology of the adoption of the UNESCO Declaration. The ban on gene therapy was in 1994, the UNESCO Declaration on the genome was adopted on 11.11.1997, the UN General Assembly in 1998, the Okinawa meeting in 2000. Section 1 of the Declaration: the human genome underlies the recognition of the unity of all people, their dignity and diversity. Article 4: the human genome in its natural state cannot be a source of income, so a part of the genome cannot be patented. Attention: 1997, that is, the adoption by UNESCO, differs from 1998, that is, the date of the UN General Assembly decision. Do not confuse the dates.

t: The genome and human dignity
n: According to Section 1 of the Declaration, the genome underlies the recognition of the unity of all people, their dignity and diversity. The genome expresses human dignity. This idea substantiates the equality and diversity of all people and of each individual. Humankind developed on the basis of a single set of genes, and genes were passed from generation to generation. Variants of genes made people diverse but of equal worth. According to Article 1 of the Declaration, the genome is regarded as the heritage of humankind. Therefore a just attitude to it is required.

t: Features of bioethics: principles are not absolute
n: On the features of bioethics. The main principles: “do no harm”, “do good”, patient autonomy and justice. None of them is an absolute criterion in assessing specific situations: each has its own sphere of application. Bioethics is a scientific and practical form of carrying out a dialogue between culture and science in the interests of the human being. Its features: a culture of dialogue, humanitarian expert review as a regulator of activity, a transdisciplinary character and the non-absolute nature of principles. In modern culture bioethics occupies a special place thanks to its transdisciplinary character and humanistic ideas.

t: Articles 2 and 4: non-discrimination and the question of patents
n: Now Articles 2 and 4. Article 2: every individual, regardless of his genetic characteristics, has the right to respect for his rights and dignity; that is, discrimination is impermissible. Article 4: the human genome in its natural state cannot give rise to financial gain. This means that a part of the genome described by a researcher cannot be patented and turned into a commercial product. Okinawa, 2000: the leaders of eight states confirmed this and declared that the genome must serve the interests of humankind.

t: Confidentiality of genetic information and the limits of research
n: The confidentiality of genetic data that make it possible to identify a person, whether stored or processed, must be protected by law. In Section C of the Declaration, the rights of a sick or healthy person are considered together with the researcher's right to pursue science. No research concerning the genome may be placed above the right, fundamental freedoms and dignity of a person or group of people. Practices that offend dignity, including cloning for the purpose of creating a human being, are not permitted. It is not scientific work but precisely this practice that is prohibited.

t: Principles in the preamble of the Declaration
n: Let us consider the principles in the preamble of the Declaration. The preamble of the UNESCO Constitution proclaims the principles of respect for the dignity of the person, the equality of human beings and mutual respect. The preamble rejects the doctrine of the inequality of nations and races. It says that the world must rest on the intellectual and moral solidarity of humankind. UNESCO is charged with developing measures against the consequences of progress in biology and genetics and with encouraging ethical research. It is noted that research on the genome must fully respect the dignity, freedoms and rights of a person or group.

t: Case analysis: genome and patent
n: Case analysis. A group of researchers has described a part of the human genome and wants to patent it and obtain commercial profit. Article 4 of the Declaration: the human genome in its natural state cannot give rise to financial gain. This means the described part of the genome cannot be patented and turned into a commercial product. The leaders of eight states confirmed this at the Okinawa meeting in 2000. Question: how do you assess this group's plan in the light of Article 4, and why?

t: Physician and patient: the parents' decision
n: In many fields of medicine the main question is determining acceptable ethical norms for the physician–patient relationship. In the field of infectious and congenital diseases, the physician works not with one patient but with a large group in which the risk of infecting others is great. Hereditary pathology is passed from parents to the child, then to generations. Many of its forms develop before the child is born, in the mother's womb, and turn out to be congenital defects. Attention: the decision about prevention or treatment is made not by the patient himself but by the pregnant woman or the parents.

t: Early detection and two interrelated problems
n: Modern biotechnology can detect a genome disorder even at a stage when there are as yet no signs of disease. Example: Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's chorea appear when a person is over 40, sometimes over 70. This situation gives rise to two interrelated ethical problems. The first is the right to know: who may know future hereditary characteristics. The second is intervention in the genotype: the limits of using the genotype. The owner of the decision is more often the pregnant woman or the parents.

t: The role of the medical worker: “Do no harm”
n: The principle “Do no harm”, inherited from Hippocrates, has become considerably more complicated today. The reason: the problems of hereditary treatment, use of embryonic tissue, prolongation of life and cloning. The chain is as follows: medical technologies expand, the benefit to the patient grows, the risk, that is, the degree of danger, also grows, and the principle “Do no harm” becomes more complicated. That is, the sphere of medical technologies has expanded: both the benefit to the patient and the degree of risk are growing.

t: Quick question: the physician and genetic information
n: Quick questions. First question: who has the right to know the future hereditary characteristics of himself, his children or his descendants? The source poses this as an ethical question that has to be resolved. Second question: why has the principle “Do no harm” become more complicated? The area of medical intervention has expanded, and together with the benefit the danger has grown. Attention, there is a risk of error: detecting a genome disorder is not the same as the presence of symptoms of disease; symptoms may be absent as yet.

t: Case analysis: asymptomatic Huntington risk
n: Case analysis. A person has no signs of disease, but a genetic test showed a risk of Huntington's chorea. Whom should the result be told to? Modern biotechnology detects a genome disorder even at a stage when there are as yet no symptoms. Example: Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's chorea. The first problem: who has and who has not the right to know the future hereditary characteristics of himself, his children, his descendants and his patients? The second problem: questions of preventing the clinical use of a particular pathological genotype and of changing it consistently.

t: Problems of biotechnology and biosafety
n: The rapid development of biomedicine and biotechnology has put extremely difficult ethical questions on the agenda. These include cloning of human cells and tissues, hereditary testing, the use of stem cells and genetic engineering. Transplantation of human organs and tissues belongs here too. The consequences of such intervention are very hard to foresee. Medical technologies have expanded and the benefit to the patient has increased, but the degree of risk has also risen. This has complicated the Hippocratic principle “Do no harm”.

t: Ethical problems brought by new technologies
n: Ethical problems brought by new technologies. First: costly medical care. Developing scientific knowledge requires great expenditure; quality medical service may become a privilege of the rich. Second: shortage of organs. Transplantology produces a shortage of donor organs; this pushes towards paid transfer of organs. Third: the price of drugs and trials, in which the rights of the trial subject may be violated. Fourth: genetic discrimination. Information about genetic diseases may be used for dismissal and refusal of insurance. Then demographic problems and the concept of life and death: technologies have changed its traditional concept, and the problem of euthanasia and artificial life-support devices has arisen.

t: Stem cells: uncertainty of risk
n: Stem cells: uncertainty of risk. Stem cells can turn into anything, so the consequences of intervention are hard to predict. The chain: a stem cell is introduced, it may turn into various tissues, there is an opinion about transfer of the donor's gene, cancer is assumed as a theoretical risk, and the long-term consequences have not been studied. Clinical studies alone are not sufficient to guarantee the safety of such intervention. They may be useful in restoring the function of the liver and brain; in joint cartilage the experience is great.

t: Prospects of stem-cell treatment
n: Prospects of stem-cell treatment. Stem cells may be useful in restoring damaged functions of the liver and brain, but the long-term consequences have not been studied. In joint cartilage there is great experience with mechanical injury, yet many aspects are still poorly studied. The idea: at birth, to create a bank from umbilical cells and in 40 to 50 years to grow an organ; this is based on the opinion of Professor Tarantul. The appearance of cancer years later, as a long-term risk, is regarded as a theoretical supposition. The long-term consequences have not been sufficiently studied; clinical studies alone do not guarantee safety.

t: Embryonic stem cells: sharp disputes
n: Research on embryonic stem cells today gives rise to sharp disputes. The hope: treatment of diseases that for the time being are incurable, such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis, and the production of organs and tissues for transplantation. Stem cells are obtained mainly from the embryo. Question: is it possible and necessary to create an artificial embryo for research? If embryos not intended for having a child are used, how can the result be determined and how can the rights of the parent donors be ensured?

t: UNESCO: three approaches to embryonic cells
n: The UNESCO committee noted three approaches to embryonic cells. According to the document, the ethical basis of research on embryonic cells depends in large part on the status of the embryo. First approach: using the embryo is contrary to morality and is rejected entirely. The second position permits it only for medical purposes and when strict conditions are met, that is, it is conditionally acceptable. Third approach: because of risk and ethical consequences the research must be prohibited.

t: Case analysis: research on embryonic stem cells
n: Case analysis. A laboratory proposes to obtain stem cells from embryos that the parents did not intend for having a child. In the document of the UNESCO International Bioethics Committee there are three approaches: entirely contrary to morality; appropriate only under strict conditions; to be prohibited because of risk. Open question: how can the result of such research be determined and how can the rights of the parent donors be ensured? The book does not object to stem-cell technology artificially grown from embryos. In Great Britain it is permitted for medical purposes.

t: The owner of genetic information and patenting
n: Question: who is the owner of hereditary information? The person who provided the material, the scientist who described it, the researcher who applied it, or the firm that provided the funds? In essence only a genuine discovery that brings benefit or is applied in industry can be patented. Article 4 of the UNESCO Declaration: the genome in its natural state is not a source of income, and a described part of the genome is not patented or commercialised. The collection, processing, storage and use of genetic data also give rise to ethical questions.

t: Data collection, biopiracy and justice
n: The question of data collection, biopiracy and justice. Does informed consent have meaning for indigenous peoples? In what language do they receive the necessary information? Follow the chain: the genetic material of a community is taken, the research gives a result, the result is patented, and the donor community is left without a share of the income. The question then arises: is this not biological piracy? Such a question is raised if the donor community does not receive a share of the income. The International Bioethics Committee proposed a special international mechanism for income from genomic information.

t: What is taken into account when collecting genetic information
n: In collecting genetic information the International Bioethics Committee pays attention to the following. First: the ultimate purpose of data collection. Second: full information is given to donors. Third: consent is voluntary and informed. Fourth: the traditional attitude of a social, religious or ethnic group to the body is taken into account. Fifth: confidentiality of data and control of subsequent use. Caution is needed in genetic tests that establish kinship. Since the genome is the heritage of humankind, the committee proposed creating a special international mechanism for income.

t: Stages of the cloning process
n: Let us look at the stages of the cloning process. First a nucleus is taken from a somatic cell. The nucleus is removed from the egg by microsurgery; this is called enucleation. Then the nucleus is introduced into the egg. After the nucleus is introduced, under the action of an electric discharge or a chemical influence the cell begins to divide and an embryo forms. Finally the embryo is transferred to a surrogate mother. The surrogate mother brings into the world a genetic twin copy of the donor.

t: Cloning: views of supporters and opponents
n: Cloning: the views of supporters and opponents. The clone is a genetic twin of the donor; it turns out to be younger than the original by several decades. Arguments of supporters: in medicine, a healthy organ for transplantation; in science, continuation of the scientific work of geniuses; in the family, the return of a child who died. Arguments of opponents: clones carry a high risk of congenital defects, genetic diversity is reduced, and the rich would use it only for themselves. In the opponents' view, genetic differences will diminish and society will become more vulnerable to epidemics. Attention: a clone is a genetic copy, but its fingerprints will be different.

t: Reproductive and therapeutic cloning
n: Reproductive and therapeutic cloning differ. Reproductive cloning is for the birth of a cloned child and is prohibited in many countries. Cloning for the purpose of creating a human being offends human dignity and is impermissible. Therapeutic cloning is for treating a serious disease; whether it can be permitted has not yet been resolved. There is concern that permission might open the way to cloning for offspring. The problem of the embryo arises again: a special embryo is created for the stem cell, and the ethical dispute continues.

t: Case analysis: cloning and the aim of treatment
n: Case analysis. It has been proposed to create a clone embryo to treat a serious incurable disease. This proposal pursues the aim of treatment. Cloning by nuclear transfer leads to the creation of an embryo intended solely for obtaining a stem cell. Question: if cloning for treatment is permitted, will this not open the way to cloning for the purpose of procreation? Attention: cloning for treatment is not the same as cloning for offspring. The international community has renounced only the aim of procreation; the former is unresolved.

t: Convergent technologies: the intersection in the source
n: Convergent technologies: the intersection in the source. Genetics, cloning and stem cells together affect medicine and society. The circle is as follows: genome and genetic diagnostics, nuclear transfer in cloning, stem cells, the possibility of treatment, ethical questions and risk. Cloning by nuclear transfer creates an embryo intended for obtaining a stem cell; this raises an ethical question.

t: Conclusion: freedom, responsibility and the physician's role
n: Let us conclude. The human gene expresses dignity; the genome cannot be a source of income, and the confidentiality of genetic data that identify a person must be protected by law. Altering the genes of germ cells is passed to offspring and is therefore prohibited for the time being. Cloning for the purpose of creating a human being is likewise impermissible. Participation in genetic research must be voluntary and the participant must have full information, that is, informed consent. New technologies have increased both the benefit and the risk; the Hippocratic principle “Do no harm” has become more complicated.
